title: Urvashi at the door
hookLine: in Indra's city, Urvashi comes to Arjuna's door at night, and he covers his eyes
carry: tapas is mastering the senses, anywhere
tomorrow: A story for a grieving king

cards: Arjuna is living in heaven. His brothers are still in the forest, and he is in Indra's city, learning the weapons of the gods. Indra has him learn music and dance as well, from the gandharva Chitrasena.
Then one evening Indra notices how Arjuna's eyes follow the apsara Urvashi, and he sends word to her. So that night, dressed for him, she comes to his door.
And the archer who fought a hunter who turned out to be Shiva does something Urvashi doesn't expect. He covers his eyes.

teach.h: "YOU ARE AN ELDER OF MY LINE."
teach.b: In the telling, Arjuna speaks to her with great respect, and what he says surprises her. You are an elder of my own line, he tells her.

Tradition says Urvashi was the mother of an ancestor of the Pandavas' house, so to Arjuna she stands where Kunti stands. He looked at her in the hall, he says, the way a child looks at an honored elder.
Urvashi answers that the apsaras are free; rules like his don't bind them. He doesn't move. And she is furious.
She curses him: he will live among women as a dancer, without his manhood. The story reaches Indra, and here it turns. Indra isn't angry; he's pleased.
He praises Arjuna's self-control and tells him the curse will serve him: when the brothers must live hidden, he'll spend that time as a dancer, and no one will look for the great archer there.
Now the teaching. On the mountain, Arjuna's tapas was fasting and enduring. Here it's a door, a night, and a no.
In Hindu tradition, tapas, the heat of discipline, isn't only for mountains; its everyday form is mastering the senses.

teach.h: THE TORTOISE DRAWS IN ITS LIMBS.
teach.b: The Bhagavad Gita pictures a tortoise drawing in its limbs: the one who can draw the senses back from what pulls them has steady wisdom.
It's why many Hindus keep a weekly fast, often Monday for Shiva. The point isn't the empty plate. It's being in charge of yourself.

how: The episode of Urvashi and Arjuna is told within the Vana Parva of the Mahabharata, and retellers often pair it with the later year in disguise, when the curse becomes Arjuna's cover.

o: Arjuna's discipline, carried from mountain to palace
the music and dance Arjuna learns in heaven
the curse that will hide Arjuna in plain sight

games.q: Arjuna in Indra's city — tap the pairs.
p: comes to Arjuna's door at night
says the curse will serve him

s: Arjuna's austerities ended once he had the weapons
his self-control was tested again in Indra's city, when Urvashi came to his door.
he said it would serve Arjuna while the brothers lived hidden, and end after that time.
in Hindu teaching, tapas also means mastering the senses, not only fasting
the Gita pictures it as a tortoise drawing in its limbs, and Arjuna kept it at Urvashi's door.

games.q: you're Arjuna, a guest in Indra's city. Urvashi comes to your door at night. what do you do?
o: cover your eyes and call her an elder of your own line.
slip away and ask Indra what to do.
games.why: he refuses her with respect: the same tapas he kept on the mountain, now as mastery of the senses. she curses him, and Indra says the curse will become his disguise.

practice: When a small pull comes as you sit, to shift, to scratch, to check the time, don't fight it and don't follow it.
Notice it rise, the way Arjuna noticed the knock at the door, and draw back, like the Gita's tortoise drawing in its limbs. Let it pass like a breath going out.
If you pray, offer each small no as part of your prayer; if not, simply sit, in charge of yourself.

wordCard.voice: Arjuna's austerities. They began on a mountain with fasting and ended in a palace with a closed door, and a curse that would one day hide him.

orig.note: Sanskrit Urvashi, the apsara who comes to Arjuna's door in Indra's city.

carryVoice: Your line: tapas is mastering the senses, anywhere. Arjuna's austerities end not on a mountain, but at a closed door. That's day seven hundred eighty-seven.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Indralokagamana sections: Arjuna in Indra's city, Chitrasena, Urvashi's curse, Indra's words)
Bhagavad Gita 2.58 (the senses drawn in like a tortoise's limbs; steady wisdom); weekly fasts (vrata), commonly Monday for Shiva
